content: 1. The GRADE system, as discussed by Coello et al., represents a developing consensus on evaluating the quality of evidence and the strength of clinical recommendations. This system is critical for ensuring that medical guidelines are based on robust and reliable data. 2. The TB-PRACTECAL trial is a pragmatic clinical study aimed at identifying more effective, concise, and less toxic treatment regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). This trial is registered under the identifier NCT02589782 and was accessed on June 21, 2021. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) published the Global Tuberculosis Report in 2020, providing comprehensive data on the global burden of tuberculosis and the progress in its management. 4. Haneuse S. highlighted the importance of distinguishing between selection bias and confounding bias in comparative effectiveness research. This distinction is crucial for ensuring the validity of study findings and their applicability to clinical practice. 5. Conradi et al. conducted a study on the treatment of highly drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020. This research provides valuable insights into managing complex cases of drug-resistant TB. 6. Johnson and Thiel discussed the implications of time until relapse in tuberculosis treatment trials for the design of phase 3 clinical trials. Their findings, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine in 2012, emphasize the need for careful consideration of relapse timing in trial protocols. 7. The WHO's 2013 revision of the definitions and reporting framework for tuberculosis provides standardized criteria for TB diagnosis, treatment outcomes, and reporting, ensuring consistency across global TB programs. 8. The WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis, Module 4, focuses on the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis. The 2020 and 2022 updates provide evidence-based recommendations for managing MDR-TB and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). 9. The WHO expert consultation in October 2020 defined extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) and provided guidance on its management. This meeting emphasized the need for tailored treatment regimens based on drug susceptibility testing. 10. The 1997 WHO guidelines for managing drug-resistant tuberculosis laid the foundation for subsequent updates, including the 2008 emergency update and the 2010 fourth edition of TB treatment guidelines. 11. The 2022 WHO guidelines introduced shorter, all-oral regimens for MDR-TB treatment, emphasizing the use of bedaquiline (Bdq), linezolid (Lzd), and fluoroquinolones (Fq) in specific combinations to improve treatment outcomes and reduce toxicity. 12. The South African TB program treats approximately 10,000 MDR/RR-TB patients annually. Data from 2017 and 2019 cohorts were analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of oral bedaquiline-based regimens, with linkage to the South African death registry to assess mortality during and after treatment. 13. Eligibility criteria for 9-12 month MDR-TB regimens include no prior exposure to second-line drugs, susceptibility to isoniazid and fluoroquinolones, and uncomplicated extrapulmonary TB. Exclusion criteria include prior second-line drug treatment, extensive disease, and resistance to key drugs like bedaquiline or linezolid. 14. The South African 2019 cohort introduced a new regimen replacing ethionamide with linezolid due to high resistance rates. This regimen demonstrated improved outcomes and was widely adopted by the end of 2019. 15. Treatment outcomes for MDR-TB include definitions for cured, treatment completed, treatment failed, died, lost to follow-up, and treatment success. Sustained treatment success is assessed at 6 and 12 months post-treatment, ensuring patients remain alive and TB-free. 16. The WHO guidelines emphasize individualized treatment for specific populations, such as children under six years, pregnant women, and patients with complicated extrapulmonary TB. Adjustments are made based on drug resistance patterns and patient-specific factors. 17. The 2022 WHO guidelines highlight the importance of monitoring adverse events, drug resistance amplification, and treatment outcomes to refine MDR-TB management strategies and improve patient care.
